# Guide for adding JusPrin tools

**Status:** This guide explains how to add a tool to JusPrin. The three things it builds on are already implemented: the shared tool registry, the MCP server embedded in the app, and the stdio bridge (a small helper program that connects external AI clients to that server). Over MCP, the tools currently cover inspecting the workspace, reporting on a slice for review, and the settings workflow. The settings workflow works on the process preset, on one object, and on filament and printer presets. Later in this guide there is a [candidate catalog](#candidate-catalog): a list of tools we might build, worked out from the product's screens. It follows the implemented catalog record. Nothing in the candidate catalog exists unless the catalog record says it does.

JusPrin has one tool system. A new capability is defined once, in the shared registry. `ToolExecutionCoordinator` runs it. Its implementation reads and changes the open project through the typed workspace interface. Two adapters, one for OpenAI and one for MCP, only translate that single definition into the format each side expects. The aim of this guide is a tool catalog that stays small, does only what it claims to do, can change safely over time, and is shaped by real printing tasks. It should not be shaped by a list of every feature OrcaSlicer has.

Treat this guide as the starting point. Change it when what you learn from implementing, from real MCP clients, or from evals shows that a rule, a contract, a limit, or a sequence here should change. Do not keep a planning assumption just because it is written here. Base every revision on evidence, and describe significant changes in the PR. Two things do not change: OrcaSlicer stays the owner of the state it owns, and the verification requirements stay.

Before you touch any OrcaSlicer class that holds live state, read [the production documentation](README.md), [production architecture](architecture.md), and [OrcaSlicer integration guide](orca-integration-guide.md). The current tool definitions are in [`ToolRegistry.cpp`](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolRegistry.cpp). The code that runs them is in [`ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp`](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/ToolExecutionCoordinator.cpp). The code that presents them over MCP is in [`McpProtocol.cpp`](../../src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Mcp/McpProtocol.cpp).

External clients on the same machine connect through the bundled `jusprin-mcp` stdio helper, which is set up from **Connect AI tools...**. The helper and the server inside the app are compiled from the same registry. So every new tool you offer must have the same catalog entry and the same schema whether the app is running (live) or not (offline), for the same build and the same negotiated protocol version. Do not add a catalog that exists in only one adapter. Connecting to the server directly over HTTP is a route for developers. It is not what the default setup instructions tell people to do.

## Words this guide uses

- **Registry.** The one list of tool definitions, compiled into the app (`ToolRegistry.cpp`).
- **Catalog.** The list of tools as a caller sees it.
- **Coordinator.** `ToolExecutionCoordinator`, the class that queues tool calls and runs them on the GUI thread.
- **Workspace.** The typed C++ interface (`IWorkspace`) through which JusPrin reads and changes the open project. It has two implementations, called workspace adapters. The real one works on live OrcaSlicer. The fake one is for tests.
- **Tool adapter.** Code that translates registry definitions and results for one kind of caller. There are two: the in-app adapter, which uses OpenAI's format and serves the Agent panel, and the MCP adapter, which serves external clients. "Both adapters" in this guide means these two.
- **Projection.** The form in which one tool adapter presents a definition or a result.
- **Exposure.** The registry setting that says which callers are offered a tool.
- **Owner.** The OrcaSlicer class that holds the real copy of some state, or that already implements an operation.
- **Seam.** A small addition to a file OrcaSlicer owns, which lets fork code call or observe OrcaSlicer's behavior.
- **Session and revision.** `sessionId` identifies the project that is currently open. `revision` is a counter the workspace raises when its state changes. A call that was prepared against an older session or revision is called stale.
- **Action class.** Whether a tool is read-only, a mutation (it changes something), or destructive.
- **Dirty.** A preset is dirty when it has unsaved edits.
- **Eval.** An automated test that gives a model a task and checks the transcript that results.
- **M0 to M5.** The milestones in which the tool catalog was delivered.

## Current connection and execution boundary

- The server starts automatically with the JusPrin Agent panel. There is no `JUSPRIN_MCP` switch to enable it and no bearer token. The server listens only on the numeric loopback address. It prefers port 47301, and falls back to a port chosen by the operating system only when 47301 is taken.
- The shell tells the server where its discovery file is: `<data_dir>/jusprin/mcp.json`. The running server writes its details there in one atomic step: the actual address, the PID, a unique `instanceId` for this run, the build version, and the protocol versions. Before a server removes the record, it checks, while holding the discovery lock, that the record is its own. An older server therefore cannot remove a newer server's record, even inside the same process. On POSIX systems the file has mode `0600`.
- The helper checks that the discovery file is valid, and then tests that the address in it answers. When the app starts or restarts later, the helper follows the new record. The helper never launches JusPrin. The discovery file holds one record, and the last server to write it wins. So the helper works with one selected instance; there is no way to choose among several. `--discovery`, `JUSPRIN_MCP_DISCOVERY`, and `JUSPRIN_MCP_URL` override the file path or the address. They do not switch anything on. The connection entries that Connect writes use `--discovery` with the app's actual data directory.
- When the app is not running, the helper answers discovery and tool-list requests from the registry compiled into the helper. Tool calls made while the app is not running return `workspace_unavailable`. When the app can be reached, the helper uses the app's live catalog and results, even when the app and the helper are different versions. Do not replace a live app's tool list with the helper's compiled one. A version difference between the two is logged.
- The HTTP adapter accepts MCP protocol version `2026-07-28`. The helper can also negotiate the older versions `2025-03-26`, `2025-06-18`, and `2025-11-25`. The helper does all conversion between versions. Code that executes a tool must not behave differently for different protocol versions.
- **Connect** shows the person the command or the file edit and asks for confirmation first. Then it either runs the Claude Code or Codex CLI, or merges the JusPrin entry into the JSON configuration of Claude Desktop/local Cowork, Cursor or VS Code. A JSON edit keeps unrelated settings and makes a backup. It is refused when the preview is out of date or when the destination is a symlink. It does not protect against another editor writing the same file at the exact moment of replacement.
- On macOS the helper is bundled next to the app executable. Windows has a matching install rule. On Linux, the entry for an AppImage uses the installed image's path plus `--mcp-bridge`, and the app handles that flag before the GUI starts. Do not save a temporary AppImage mount path as the command.

Workspace commands run on the GUI thread, through the shared coordinator. A timer owned by the shell keeps execution moving, so execution does not depend on the WebView's handshake. No external client ever gets direct access to OrcaSlicer objects.

A call from an external client is tagged `ToolSource::Mcp`. The MCP adapter sets that tag, so it can be trusted, and it is kept for the activity history and for diagnostics. External calls run through the same coordinator and the same workspace commands as calls from the in-app Agent. The change log records the edits they make, as it records every edit, and marks them `external`. In the conversation thread those edits appear as rows that say "External tool", where a change made in the app says "Agent".

## Start with an eval failure

The fact that OrcaSlicer has a menu item or a config key is not a reason to add a tool. Start from a transcript or an automated eval in which the Agent cannot finish a real user task, finishes it only some of the time, or needs an unreasonable number of steps or tokens.

Write down:

- what the user wanted to achieve;
- the exact point where the current tools stop being enough;
- which OrcaSlicer state or operation is missing;
- what a successful transcript should look like;
- the unsafe or ambiguous cases that must fail; and
- the evidence that will show the new tool fixed the problem.

If the failure can be fixed by a clearer description, a better result, or a more useful validation error, improve the existing definition instead of adding a tool.

The candidate catalog later in this guide lists tools we might build. Being listed there does not accept a tool, and it does not excuse a tool from this section. A row in that catalog does two jobs. It records which product screen and which group of evals the tool would serve, which makes the eval easier to write. It also settles what the tool acts on, its action class, and its OrcaSlicer owner, so that two people do not build the same capability twice under different names.

## Decide whether this should be a tool

Add or extend a tool when the Agent needs one of three things: up-to-date state read straight from OrcaSlicer, a calculation that OrcaSlicer does and that always gives the same answer for the same input, or a change to the live project.

Do not add a tool for:

- a single setting key. Setting keys are records that the generic settings tools search and edit;
- general printing advice that the model can work out from a skill;
- a fixed bundle of changes such as "make it stronger", where the right answer depends on the part and on what the user cares about;
- driving the UI, such as pressing a button or operating a widget or a hidden panel;
- data that an existing tool already returns in a size-limited result;
- a capability someone might want in the future, with no eval or user task behind it; or
- an operation that the real workspace adapter cannot truly perform through the OrcaSlicer class that owns it.

A fixed, mechanical step of a workflow can be a tool. Examples are generating OrcaSlicer's calibration geometry and starting OrcaSlicer's slice action. Advice should stay a skill until there is a separately specified operation behind it that always behaves the same way.

## Skills versus tools

A skill is text the model reads. A tool is something the app executes. To decide which one a candidate is, ask one question: does it have to run, or does it only have to be read?

- It has to run if it reads state the model does not have, computes something only OrcaSlicer can compute, or changes the project. That makes it a tool.
- It only has to be read if it is judgement, the order to do things in, facts about printing, how to interpret a tool's result, or which question to ask first. That makes it a skill.

The section above covers tools. This section covers skills, and decides the cases that fall in between.

A skill contains things the model could do by itself if it had the right knowledge. It contains nothing that executes. Examples:

- judging evidence, such as telling an adhesion failure from wet filament in a photo;
- the order of a series of tool calls, and the reasons for that order. For "make it stronger": read the settings, change walls and infill, slice, read the report;
- facts about printing, such as what PETG tolerates;
- which question to ask when the answer would change the plan.

A skill is a file on the Agent page, `AgentUI/src/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`: frontmatter with its `name` and a `trigger`, a `description` or both, then the text the model gets. The page sends every skill once per connection with the `skills` bridge message. A skill with a trigger is the app's: when the event it names happens, the host adds it to the one request where the model first reads about the event, as the request's last item, and to no later request. A skill with a description is the model's: `skill_read` lists the described skills in its own description and returns one by name, and is offered only while at least one exists (none does yet). Four skills have triggers, one file each:

- `file-loaded` (trigger `file_loaded`): the first message after a file is opened or imported is a judgement about the load report. It fires when the person opens or drops a file, after an in-app `object_import` (and a failed `project_open`) in the same turn, and in the opened project's chat after an in-app `project_open`, which replaces the conversation and so ends the turn that asked. An MCP client's loads fire nothing. The host sends a picture of the active plate with it and, when no purpose is recorded, one sentence of its own built from that state.
- `project-setup-changed` (trigger `setup_changed`): check the setup in force against the print's purpose. It fires on the result of an in-app `intent_update` that recorded a purpose for the first time or changed it (its result says which in `purposeChange`), when the printer, filament, process or plate type differs from the setup the model was last asked to check under a recorded purpose (on the next tool result of the turn, or on the next turn's first request when the person changed it by hand), and on a turn's first request after the person restored an earlier version while a purpose is recorded. Each time the model is asked to check, the app saves the setup in force as the one checked. The model's own successful `printer_setup` fires nothing: the setup it chose is saved as checked at once (Kenneth, 2026-10-19), so the skill is for a setup that moved without the model, and a pairing its change breaks is caught by the slice-refusal facts and skill. It gives way to the file-loaded skill on a request that carries both, since that skill already asks for the same check.
- `slice-failed` (trigger `slice_failed`): a plate's last slice did not succeed, because OrcaSlicer's check refused the plate or the run failed. The adapter records why on the plate (`WorkspacePlate::slice_failure`: refused or failed, OrcaSlicer's words, the setting and object when named) at the moment it happens (a hook in `Plater::reslice`, `Workspace/SliceRequests.hpp`, and the run's completion event), worded by the print-issue monitor's `slice_failure_of`, and keeps it until the plate slices. Every request carries it as the plate's `sliceFailure`; `slice_report` of an unsliced plate adds the check code and the object's name. The skill fires once per failure, on the first request that carries it: the result of the model's own `slice_start`, the turn the app starts when a slice the model started fails after its turn, or the next message after the person's Slice all. The same refusal again is the same failure.
- `print-issues` (trigger `print_issues`): what the print-issue chip's two buttons ask for and how to read what OrcaSlicer reports. The adapter reads a slice's warnings through the monitor's `slice_warnings_of` while the plate is active and keeps a summary on the plate while that slice is current (`WorkspacePlate::slice_warnings`: the count, how many the person ignored, and the first warning, critical first, in OrcaSlicer's words with its setting and object). It counts every warning the chip lists, so the bed-temperature warning too, which `slice_report` leaves out. Every request carries it as the plate's `sliceWarnings`. The skill fires on the request that carries a chip's message, and on the first request whose workspace shows warnings no request has carried yet, whether the person sliced (their next message) or the model did (the tool result that shows them, or the app's turn when its slice ended after its turn); a re-slice with the same warnings fires nothing.

The cases in between:

- **A procedure made of existing tool calls.** It is a skill for as long as carrying it out takes judgement. It becomes a tool only when the steps are fixed and the person wants the whole thing as one action that can be undone. If there are many such fixed sequences, they go in one workflow registry (see [When resources or skills are appropriate](#when-resources-or-skills-are-appropriate)).
- **An analysis.** It is a tool when OrcaSlicer computes it and always gets the same answer, such as overhang angles from geometry. It is a skill when it is a judgement about evidence. Pair that skill with the tool that supplies the evidence (`view_render`, `slice_report`).
- **Large reference data.** When the model needs only one part of the data, make it a tool that returns the part an argument selects, as `settings_search` does. When the model needs to see all of the data before it can use any of it, make it text. The printer list described under [Input design](#input-design) is the case we measured: putting the whole list in the instructions worked better than the search tool.
- **A tool description versus a skill.** A tool description says when to call that one tool, in the words a person would use. A skill says how several tools fit together and what to conclude from their results. If a tool description has grown into a step-by-step procedure, move the procedure out into a skill.

When you are not sure, start with a skill. A skill is a text file that ships with the page. A tool costs the whole implementation sequence described below, including fakes, tests, and rebase evidence. Turn a skill into a tool only on the kind of evidence every tool starts from (see [Start with an eval failure](#start-with-an-eval-failure)). Either transcripts show the model getting the sequence wrong in ways that better text does not fix, or the action needs something only the app can give: all-or-nothing application, validation, or undo. The opposite sign exists too. If a skill has turned into exact values and calls in a fixed order, with no judgement between them, it should be written as a tool.

How something gets loaded into the model's context does not decide whether it is a skill or a tool. Today a skill costs its one line in the instructions, and a tool costs its definition on the first request of a conversation (see [Tool budget and tool shape](#tool-budget-and-tool-shape)). If we later use the model platform's deferred loading, both will cost one index line plus a load when needed. A skill could then be a deferred read-only tool: the tool's description is the skill's index line, and the tool's result is the skill's text. Tools and skills would then be found the same way and covered by the same eval.

## Prefer extending nouns over multiplying verbs

The settings workflow has four operations that do not change. They work on searchable data, whichever preset layer the values belong to:

```text
settings_search → settings_get → settings_preview_patch → settings_apply_patch
```

Do not create one tool per setting:

```text
set_layer_height
set_wall_loops
set_infill_density
set_support_angle
```

The same rule applies to presets, project objects, plates, warnings, and slice reports. Extend the typed records that describe them, and the size-limited tools that query them, before you create dozens of special-purpose actions.

A new operation deserves its own tool when it really differs from the existing ones in at least one of these ways: which action class it belongs to (read-only, mutation or destructive), whether it applies completely or not at all, how it starts, runs, and ends, or what its result means. `slice_start` is an example. It is not one more way to change settings. It starts OrcaSlicer work that runs in the background, and it completes in a different way from a settings change. That difference justifies a separate tool.

Split an operation into a preview tool and an apply tool only where OrcaSlicer may rewrite, replace, or refuse what the caller asked for. In those cases the caller has to see what would really happen before submitting the change. There are four such cases:

- settings, because OrcaSlicer's normalizer (the code that adjusts dependent settings after an edit) can rewrite values;
- preset selection, because OrcaSlicer may substitute a compatible preset, and dirty edits may be lost;
- topology changes such as cutting, splitting, or merging, because the caller needs to see the resulting pieces;
- preflight (the check before a print is sent), because of filament mapping and printer readiness.

Everywhere else, the coordinator computes and validates the resulting state as part of the call. If a preview would only repeat its input back, do not make it a tool.

Prefer read tools whose results have a fixed, typed shape. Avoid one general record search whose result changes shape. Each section of `workspace_inspect` keeps its own fixed shape. A generic `records_search` whose result shape depends on a `kind` argument would make the model guess what comes back.

## Tool budget and tool shape

The limit on the number of tools comes from how much the model has to load on each turn. It does not come from how much the app can do. The rules in this section rest on this evidence:

- OpenAI's function-calling guidance keeps fewer than 20 functions available at the start of a turn and defers the rest.
- Anthropic's [tool-writing guidance](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents) asks for a few tools aimed at high-impact workflows. It names "tools that merely wrap existing software functionality or API endpoints" as the common error.
- A [domain-oriented MCP study](https://arxiv.org/html/2608.22063v1) measured three interfaces. A generic interface of thin tools scored below raw SQL. Tools shaped around the domain scored far above both.
- The "god tool", one tool that dispatches many unrelated actions through a single `action` parameter, is a documented anti-pattern.

The current five-tool MCP catalog measures about 1.9 KB per definition, and two thirds of that is output schema.

**How tools are loaded for now.** Both adapters load every registered tool on every turn. The in-app adapter sends the full function list with each request, and MCP `tools/list` returns the whole catalog. This is the simplest behaviour that is correct. It also keeps the tools array byte-identical through a chat, and OpenAI's prompt cache depends on exactly that. The budget is 20 definitions per turn. Going over 20 does not block anything. It is the point at which we start watching the measurements. The live regression test records definition bytes, input tokens, and cached tokens for each request. The journey catalog below goes over 20 definitions from its first milestone. We accept that until those measurements show the model selecting wrong tools or running short of context.

**The baseline, measured on Windows against the live app.**

| After milestone | In-app definitions | In-app bytes | MCP definitions | MCP bytes | MCP bytes through the offline helper recipe |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| M0 | 7 | 3,145 | 5 | 3,147 | |
| M1 | 11 | 6,482 | 9 | 6,915 | |
| M2 | 18 | 12,721 | 16 | 13,911 | 13,894 |
| M3 | 20 | 19,331 | 21 | 22,661 | 22,639 |
| M4 | 20 | 21,594 | 21 | 24,923 | 24,901 |
| M5 | 25 | 29,148 | 26 | 33,013 | |

The M5 figure for MCP was read over two `tools/list` pages.

The `--live-agent` regression test, run at M0 and at M1, shows what those definitions cost in tokens. The first request of a conversation gets nothing from the cache and pays for the whole catalog: 803 tokens at M0 and 1,733 at M1. So four more definitions cost about 930 tokens, paid once. Every later request in the same conversation came back 77 to 92 per cent cached (at M1, 5,864 input tokens, of which 5,376 were cached). That is because the tools array is byte-identical through a chat, and the cache depends on that. At M2, the same test made eleven requests that took 2,875 to 6,763 input tokens, with 42 to 91 per cent cached. None of the eleven started with an empty cache, because an earlier run on the same day had already cached the shared beginning of the prompt. So that run did not measure the uncached cost at M2.

The conclusion is that a definition adds cost to the *first* request of each conversation, not to every turn. That is why going over the budget only makes us look at the measurements and does not block a tool. Two things would change this conclusion: a catalog so large that the first request of every conversation is expensive by itself, or transcripts that show the model choosing the wrong tool. Watch for both. Neither has appeared yet.

**The printer panel follows the same rule with its own set of tools.** The printer panel on Home runs its own conversation, `PrinterConversation`. That conversation is offered the five printer tools and the four settings tools. The list is the same in every mode (Add, Change, or Connect), so it stays byte-identical through a conversation and between conversations of the same mode.

What a call may do depends on the conversation. `PrinterConversation::preflight_tool` refuses every call that is not allowed, before any card is shown, with an error that says where to go instead. The rules are:

- Finding and adding a printer (`printer_identify`, `printer_add`) is allowed only in an Add conversation. A Change or Connect conversation is about a printer the person already has. An add there would save another printer and move the conversation onto it.
- `printer_change` is allowed only on the printer the conversation is about, once there is one. When the project uses that printer, its unsaved edits are dropped and listed in `discarded`; the panel's coordinator saves a version first, as the project's agent pane does for any change to the project. If that save fails, the call does not run and returns the coordinator's generic `local_save_failed`; there is no separate message for it.
- The connection tools are allowed only once there is a saved printer.

entries.name: WebFetch
entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

entries.name: WebSearch
entries.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

OpenRouter does expose a Responses API at the `/api/v1/responses` path. The official docs describe it as OpenRouter's OpenAI-compatible Responses API. Stateless transformation layer with support for reasoning, tool calling, and web search. The create endpoint accepts a streaming or non-streaming response using OpenResponses API format, sent as a POST to `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/responses` with a bearer token.

Usage examples show the `input` field as either a plain string or a list of structured message items, along with optional parameters such as `reasoning`, `max_output_tokens`, and `plugins` for web search. One docs page is labeled "Beta" in its title, so the API may still be evolving.

A Portkey gateway issue reports that the OpenRouter provider there currently only supports chatComplete. That issue is about 243 days old, so it likely predates the current docs and may be out of date.

The official docs list a few concrete limitations, and the search didn't surface much detail on streaming.

- **Tool use:** The `strict` parameter for function calling is ignored, so tool-call JSON isn't guaranteed to match your schema. For guaranteed conformance, Anthropic points to its native API with Structured Outputs. The strict parameter for function calling is ignored, which means the tool use JSON is not guaranteed to follow the supplied schema. A separate, Chinese-language reference table lists `parallel_tool_calls` as fully supported.
- **System messages:** Anthropic accepts only one initial system message, so multiple system or developer messages get merged into a single system message at the start of the conversation. The API takes all system/developer messages and concatenates them together with a single newline (\n) in between them. This full string is then supplied as a single system message at the start of the messages.
- **Silently ignored fields:** Most unsupported fields are silently ignored rather than producing errors. Audio input is ignored and stripped, and prompt caching is unsupported on this endpoint, though it works in the native Anthropic SDKs.
- **Other gaps:** The `n` parameter must be exactly 1, and the endpoint has no embeddings support. Temperature is capped at 1, and the Chinese reference table marks many OpenAI-specific fields as ignored, including `logprobs`, `seed`, and `response_format`.
- **Thinking:** You can enable extended thinking through the `thinking` parameter, but the OpenAI SDK won't return Claude's detailed thought process.
- **Rate limits:** Rate limits follow Anthropic's standard limits for the /v1/messages endpoint.
- **Intended use:** Anthropic describes the layer as primarily intended to test and compare model capabilities, and is not considered a long-term or production-ready solution for most use cases.

I didn't find a specific streaming limitation in these results. The Chinese reference table marks `stream` and `stream_options` as fully supported. Check the official page's streaming section for details.

83:**Per-turn reminders in a tool loop: turn-scoped messages, never deleted.** A reminder injected into history and removed on the next request is a history edit - the cache misses from that point and, on Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Haiku 5.5, every later thinking block is invalidated. Instead give the `role: "system"` message `clear_at: "next_user_message"` (beta `mid-conversation-system-clear-at-2026-08-21`; same models and platforms as mid-conversation system messages): it renders for one turn, then stays in the transcript cleared - costing no input tokens, not cache-eligible (`cache_control` on it is a 400; put the breakpoint on the preceding user turn), and still part of the prefix. Append a fresh copy after each `tool_result` message and leave earlier copies in place; without the beta, a `text` block after the `tool_result` blocks in the same user message, earlier copies kept. Separately, per-message effort (beta `mid-conversation-output-config-2026-07-01`; Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Haiku 5.5 with thinking on; Claude API and Google Cloud): a `role: "system"` message with `content: []` and `output_config: {effort: ...}` changes effort from the next user turn on **without** the messages-cache invalidation that a top-level `effort` change causes, and is exempt from the placement rules (it can sit anywhere) - see the Invalidation hierarchy below and `shared/model-migration.md` -> Migrating to Claude Fable 5.1 from Claude Fable 5 -> New API features.

87-Don't cache. If the first 1K tokens differ per request, there is no reusable prefix. Adding `cache_control` only pays the cache-write premium with zero reads. Leave it off.

91-## Architectural guidance
92-
93-These are the decisions that matter more than marker placement. Fix these first.
94-
95-**Keep the system prompt frozen.** Don't interpolate "current date: X", "mode: Y", "user name: Z" into the system prompt - those sit at the front of the prefix and invalidate everything downstream. Inject dynamic context later in `messages` instead - as a `{"role": "system", ...}` message where supported (see § Mid-conversation system messages above), or as text in a user message otherwise. A message at turn 5 invalidates nothing before turn 5.
--
204:If `cache_creation_input_tokens` is instead near the full conversation size on every request, either the prefix is being rewritten upstream of the breakpoint, or the write is happening for a reason payload diffing and cache diagnostics can't localize - with thinking enabled on a model that strips prior-turn thinking blocks the invalidation is server-side (§ Invalidation hierarchy), and a single turn that appends more than 20 positions (parallel tool-call runs collapse to one position - § 20-block lookback window) pushes the previous entry out of the lookback so every request rewrites the whole conversation with byte-identical payloads (§ 20-block lookback window). Rule both show-nothing cases out first from the model and the turn shape. Reads can only land on positions where a previous request wrote a breakpoint, so the usage fields say *that* the prefix broke (reads collapse, often to zero) but not where - the payload diff or cache diagnostics below localizes the exact point.
205-
206-**Finding the invalidator.** Log several consecutive request payloads (the full JSON body) and diff adjacent pairs. In a growing conversation, adjacent payloads legitimately differ at the end (the newly appended turn); what must be byte-identical is the overlap - the previous request's prompt should reappear unchanged as a prefix of the next. Strip `cache_control` markers before diffing: the moving marker always differs between adjacent requests and is not an invalidator (previously-marked blocks are still cache hits). The first remaining divergence inside the overlapping region is the invalidation point. This catches the class of bug code review misses - nondeterministic serialization, a library reordering keys or fields, a value that changes between requests but not within one. On the Claude API, cache diagnostics (beta header `cache-diagnosis-2026-04-07`) does this comparison server-side once you opt in: send the header on **every** request - fingerprints are stored only for requests that carried it, so a one-shot retrofit fails with `previous_message_not_found` - then pass the previous response's `id` as `diagnostics.previous_message_id` and the response's `diagnostics` object names where the two requests diverged (model, system, tools, or message history). No payload logging needed. Availability: `shared/platform-availability.md`.
207-
208-**Unexplained writes:** `usage.cache_creation` breaks `cache_creation_input_tokens` down by TTL (`ephemeral_5m_input_tokens` / `ephemeral_1h_input_tokens`). Server tools such as web search automatically insert a 5-minute cache write after tool results when the request already uses caching - writes at a position you didn't mark; expected behavior, not an invalidator.
209-
210----
211-
212:## Invalidation hierarchy
213-
214-Not every parameter change invalidates everything. The API has three cache tiers, and changes only invalidate their own tier and below:
215-
216-| Change | Tools cache | System cache | Messages cache |
217-|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|
218-| Tool definitions (add/remove/reorder) | No | No | No |
219-| Model switch | No | No | No |
220-| `speed`, web-search, citations toggle | Yes | No | No |
221-| System prompt content | Yes | No | No |
222-| `tool_choice`, images | Yes | Yes | No |
223-| `thinking` or `effort` change | model-specific | model-specific | No |
224-| Message content | Yes | Yes | No |
--
293:**Match the real traffic's thinking and effort settings.** Both are rendered into the prompt (see § Invalidation hierarchy), so a pre-warm with different settings can write a cache entry your real traffic never hits. For adaptive-thinking traffic, send the same `thinking` and `effort` values in the pre-warm. Traffic that uses extended thinking (`thinking.type: "enabled"`, accepted only on Claude 4.6 and earlier models and on Claude Mythos Preview) can't be matched, because `max_tokens: 0` rejects that setting (see Rejected combinations below). Whether a pre-warm still helps that traffic depends on where the model renders the thinking configuration, which the docs don't state per model - check `cache_read_input_tokens` on the first real request.
294-
295-**Rejected combinations:** `max_tokens: 0` is an `invalid_request_error` with `stream: true`, `thinking.type: "enabled"`, `output_config.format`, `tool_choice` of `{"type":"tool"}` or `{"type":"any"}`, or inside a Message Batches request.

The page's **JSON Schema limitations** section has three parts: supported features, unsupported features, and regex pattern support. Here they are, mapped to your list:

**Supported keywords and types**
- All basic types: object, array, string, integer, number, boolean, null
- `enum` (strings, numbers, bools, or nulls only)
- `const`
- `anyOf` and `allOf` (with limitations: "`allOf` with `$ref` not supported")
- `$ref`, `$def`, and `definitions` (external `$ref` not supported)
- `default` for all supported types
- `required` and `additionalProperties` (must be `false` for objects)
- String formats: `date-time`, `time`, `date`, `duration`, `email`, `hostname`, `uri`, `ipv4`, `ipv6`, `uuid`
- Array `minItems` (only 0 and 1)

**Unsupported features**
- Recursive schemas
- Complex types within enums
- External `$ref` (for example, `'$ref': 'http://...'`)
- Numerical constraints (`minimum`, `maximum`, `multipleOf`)
- String constraints (`minLength`, `maxLength`)
- Array constraints beyond `minItems` of 0 or 1
- `additionalProperties` set to anything other than `false`

Using an unsupported feature returns a 400 error with details.

**Specific constraints**
- **additionalProperties:** Must be `false` for objects.
- **required:** Supported. The output orders required properties first, then optional ones.
- **enum:** Only strings, numbers, bools, or nulls. Casing isn't guaranteed: "Claude may return a value that differs from your schema only in capitalization." Compare case-insensitively.
- **Numeric constraints (`minimum`, `maximum`, `multipleOf`):** Not supported. SDK helpers can move them into the field description and, for some helpers, validate responses against them. For example, `minimum: 100` becomes a plain integer in the sent schema, with `{minimum: 100}` added to the description.
- **String formats:** Only the ten listed above are supported. The SDK helpers filter other formats out.
- **pattern (regex):** Supported: anchors (`^...$`), quantifiers (`*`, `+`, `?`, simple `{n,m}`), character classes (`[]`, `.`, `\d`, `\w`, `\s`), and groups `(...)`. Not supported: backreferences (`\1`), lookahead/lookbehind, `\b`/`\B`, and complex `{n,m}` with large ranges. "Simple regex patterns work well. Complex patterns may result in 400 errors."
- **Recursion:** Recursive schemas are not supported.
- **Nesting limits:** The page doesn't state a fixed nesting depth limit. It warns that "Deeply nested objects with optional fields compound the complexity" and advises flattening structures where possible. Nesting also counts toward the compiled-grammar complexity limits, which return "Schema is too complex for compilation" errors.
- **definitions/$ref:** `$ref`, `$def`, and `definitions` are supported for internal references. External `$ref` (such as `http://...`) is not. `allOf` combined with `$ref` is also not supported.

**Example: a schema that stays within these limits**

```json
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "name": { "type": "string" },
    "email": { "type": "string", "format": "email" },
    "tags": { "type": "array", "items": { "type": "string" }, "minItems": 1 },
    "status": { "enum": ["active", "inactive"] }
  },
  "required": ["name", "email"],
  "additionalProperties": false
}
```

# Design: Anthropic, OpenRouter and other LLM APIs behind one agent loop

Written 2026-10-19 on `jusprin-newui`. Working document, untracked.

## Summary

JusPrin's in-app agent talks to exactly one API today: OpenAI's Responses API, through `OpenAIResponsesAgent` (613 lines). That class does three jobs at once: it runs the tool-call turn loop, it builds and parses the Responses wire format, and it holds OpenAI-specific choices such as which tools get `strict: true`. Setup, configuration and three test harnesses are hard-wired to that class and to that wire format.

The proposal is to split the class into a provider-neutral turn loop plus one small "codec" per API family, and to describe each provider as data (endpoint, auth header, default model, error wording). After the split, OpenRouter costs one data entry because it serves an OpenAI-compatible Responses endpoint. Anthropic costs one codec file of roughly 350 lines plus a schema projection. Any later OpenAI-compatible host (Groq, Together, Ollama, a local proxy) costs a data entry, or a third codec if it only speaks Chat Completions.

The MCP server needs no change. It shares only the tool registry with the LLM side, and the registry stays the single definition of every tool. One shared constraint did turn up: the registry's schemas use keywords that Anthropic's strict mode rejects, and the fix belongs in the Anthropic codec, not the registry.

## What exists today

| Piece | File | Provider-neutral? |
|---|---|---|
| `IAgentService`: start a turn, continue after a tool result, poll typed events | `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/AgentService.hpp` | Yes |
| `AgentRequest`, `AgentConversationContext`: instructions, workspace, attachments, skills, earlier calls with their results | same | Yes |
| `IAgentHttpTransport`: one streaming POST, events queued to the GUI thread | `OpenAIResponsesAgent.hpp`, `OpenAIHttpTransport.cpp` | Yes, except the request carries a single `authorization` string |
| Turn loop: queue a response's calls, run one at a time, answer later ones unrun after a failure, refuse unknown or invalid calls (two per turn), send images after results, send fired skills once, report usage, cancellation generations | `OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp` | Yes in substance, but written against Responses JSON |
| Wire format: `instructions`, `input[]` items, `function_call` / `function_call_output`, SSE `response.*` events, `store:false`, `strict` per tool | `OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp` | No |
| Within-turn history: the raw `output[]` of each response, re-sent on every continuation | `m_input_history` | No. Carries OpenAI reasoning items, which must be echoed verbatim |
| Across-turn history: text plus call/result pairs, rebuilt by the host from the project document | `AgentHost.cpp` around line 2480 | Yes |
| Setup probe: one real request through the adapter | `AgentSetup.cpp` | Hard-codes `OpenAIResponsesAgent` |
| Runtime wiring and the `JUSPRIN_OPENAI_ENDPOINT` override | `AgentConfiguration.cpp` | Hard-codes `openai` |
| Setup page provider list | `AgentUI/src/components/Setup.tsx` | Lists Anthropic and Other as unavailable |
| Tool registry and MCP projection | `ToolRegistry.cpp`, `Mcp/McpProtocol.cpp` | Yes |

Three test surfaces read the Responses wire format directly: the 33 adapter tests in `tests/agent/test_openai_responses_agent.cpp`, the shell harness modes that record or hold request bodies (`tests/shell/shell_harness.cpp`, `project_prompt_scenario.inc`), and the Python prompt evals (`tests/project_prompt`, `tests/printer_prompt`), which replay recorded bodies against OpenRouter's Responses endpoint.

## Facts that decide the shape

Verified against current documentation on 2026-10-19:

- **OpenRouter serves a Responses API** at `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/responses`. It is stateless and rejects `store: true` and `previous_response_id`. The adapter already sends `store: false` and replays the full turn, so the current request bodies are already in the shape OpenRouter wants. Tool calls use the same `function_call` / `function_call_output` items. The reasoning page is labelled beta. ([overview](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/responses/overview), [tool calling](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/responses/tool-calling))
- **Anthropic's OpenAI-compatible endpoint is not a shortcut.** Anthropic's own page says it ignores `strict`, drops prompt caching, merges every system message into one, and is meant for testing, not production. ([OpenAI SDK compatibility](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/cli-sdks-libraries/libraries/openai-sdk)) Anthropic needs its native Messages API.
- **Anthropic strict mode rejects schema keywords the registry uses.** Unsupported: `minimum`, `maximum`, `multipleOf`, `minLength`, `maxLength`, and array constraints other than `minItems` of 0 or 1. The registry's schemas contain `maxItems` 55 times, `minimum` 13, `maxLength` 13, `maximum` 5, and one `minItems: 2`. A strict request with any of them is a 400. ([structured outputs limitations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs)) OpenAI accepts these keywords today; the live harness runs prove it.
- **Within one turn, both APIs need the assistant's output echoed verbatim.** OpenAI returns reasoning items with `encrypted_content` under `store: false` and asks for them back with the function outputs. ([reasoning guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning)) Anthropic wants the full `content[]` of the assistant message, thinking blocks included, and on Claude Opus 5.5 and later a changed earlier turn invalidates thinking blocks. The within-turn history therefore has to stay provider-shaped and opaque to the loop.
- **Across turns, both APIs accept a neutral record.** Text messages plus call/result pairs render as `function_call` + `function_call_output` on Responses and as an assistant `tool_use` block followed by a user `tool_result` block on Anthropic. The host already persists exactly this neutral record.
- **The current Claude models reject things the adapter never uses.** Forced `tool_choice`, assistant prefill, and `thinking: {type: "disabled"}` all return 400 on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5. The adapter uses none of them, so the Anthropic codec simply omits `thinking` and `tool_choice`.

## Proposed structure

```
IAgentService                      (unchanged)
  ProviderAgent                    the turn loop; today's OpenAIResponsesAgent minus the wire format
    IProviderCodec                 one per API family, pure JSON in and out, no network, no GUI
      ResponsesCodec               OpenAI, OpenRouter, any Responses-compatible host
      AnthropicCodec               Messages API
      ChatCompletionsCodec         later, only if a Chat-Completions-only host is wanted
    ProviderProfile                data: family, endpoint, auth style, default model, extra headers, error wording
    IAgentHttpTransport            unchanged, except headers become a list instead of one authorization string
```

### The loop and the transcript it owns

`ProviderAgent` keeps every rule the current class enforces, unchanged: one call runs at a time in the order written; a failed call answers the rest unrun; an unknown or invalid call is refused back to the model at most twice per turn; a result's image follows the results; fired skills ride on one request only; usage goes to the listener; a late event from a cancelled request is dropped by generation. All of that is expressed over a neutral transcript:

```
TurnTranscript
  instructions                      the session's text, byte-identical across the chat
  tools                             the ToolDefinitions offered this turn, plus skill_read's list
  opening                           earlier conversation (neutral records) + this turn's user content
  steps[]                           one per response so far:
    assistant_turn   json           opaque: output[] for Responses, content[] for Anthropic
    results[]                       call_id, state, output_json, optional image
    once[]                          skills fired by those results, sent on the next request only
```

The loop never looks inside `assistant_turn`. It gets the calls, the text deltas, the usage and the stop state from the codec's parsed events, and hands the opaque turn back to the same codec on the next request. A turn never changes provider, so the opaque value is always read by the codec that wrote it.

### The codec interface

Two functions, both deterministic and testable without a transport:

- `build(const TurnTranscript&, const ProviderProfile&, RequestKind) -> {body json, headers}`. `RequestKind` is the normal reply or the conversation-title request.
- `parse(const std::string& sse_data_payload) -> std::vector<StreamEvent>`. The loop keeps the SSE framing (it is identical across all three families) and passes each `data:` payload in. Events are neutral: `TextDelta`, `TurnComplete{assistant_turn, calls[], usage, stop}`, `Incomplete`, `Failed{code, retryable}`.

Anthropic's stream needs per-index accumulation of `input_json_delta` fragments before a call exists, so a codec is an object with a small amount of per-response state, reset by the loop at each request.

### Where each difference lives

| Concern | ResponsesCodec (OpenAI, OpenRouter) | AnthropicCodec | ChatCompletionsCodec (later) |
|---|---|---|---|
| System prompt | `instructions` | top-level `system` with a `cache_control` breakpoint | first message, role system |
| App notes mid-conversation (today's developer role) | role `developer` | role `system` inside `messages` (Opus 5, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable; no beta header); for older models, a user text in the app's tag | role `system` on OpenAI; a tagged user text elsewhere, since hosts differ |
| Tool definition | `{type:function, name, parameters, strict}` | `{name, description, input_schema, strict}`, `cache_control` on the last tool | `{type:function, function:{...}}` |
| Strict | registry schema as is, `strict` when the object tree is closed (today's rule) | project the schema: move `minimum`, `maximum`, `minLength`, `maxLength`, `maxItems` and `minItems` above 1 into the property description, then `strict: true` | off by default; hosts vary |
| Tool result | `function_call_output` with a string `output` | `tool_result` with text and image blocks in one user message, all results of a response together | role `tool` messages, one per call |
| Image beside a result | separate user message after the results | image block inside the `tool_result` | separate user message |
| PDF attachment | `input_file` | `document` block, base64 | OpenRouter `file` part; otherwise text only |
| Streaming text | `response.output_text.delta` | `content_block_delta` with `text_delta` | `choices[0].delta.content` |
| Streaming calls | complete items in `response.completed` | `content_block_start` type `tool_use`, then `input_json_delta` fragments by index | `delta.tool_calls[i]` fragments by index |
| Terminal | `response.completed`, `incomplete`, `failed` | `message_delta` carries `stop_reason` and output usage; `message_stop` ends | `finish_reason` |
| Stop states | completed, incomplete | `end_turn`, `tool_use`, `max_tokens` (Incomplete), `refusal` (Failed, not retryable, with the category), `pause_turn` (resend) | `stop`, `tool_calls`, `length` |
| Usage | `input_tokens`, `input_tokens_details.cached_tokens` | `input_tokens`, `cache_read_input_tokens`, `cache_creation_input_tokens`, `output_tokens` | `prompt_tokens`, `prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`, with `stream_options.include_usage` |
| Prompt cache | automatic on a stable prefix | explicit: breakpoint on the last tool, the system text, and the last user message; tools, then system, then messages is the invalidation order | automatic on OpenAI; passed through on OpenRouter |
| Thinking | provider default | omit `thinking`; depth through `output_config.effort` from the profile | none |
| Required fields | none | `max_tokens` | none |
| Auth and version | `Authorization: Bearer` | `x-api-key`, `anthropic-version: 2023-06-01` | `Authorization: Bearer` |
| Idempotency | `Idempotency-Key` header | not documented; send nothing | not documented; send nothing |
| Errors | 401/403, 429, 5xx, timeout | the same plus 529 overloaded (retryable) and 413 | the same |

Error text today names OpenAI ("The OpenAI API key was rejected"). The display name moves into `ProviderProfile` so the wording is right for every provider without a per-provider branch.

### Provider profiles

A static table, one row per provider the setup page offers, plus a "custom" row the user fills in:

| id | family | endpoint | auth | default model |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| openai | responses | `https://api.openai.com/v1/responses` | bearer | `gpt-5.4-mini` (today's) |
| openrouter | responses | `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/responses` | bearer, plus `HTTP-Referer` and `X-Title` identifying JusPrin | to be chosen; the prompt evals use `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash` |
| anthropic | anthropic | `https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages` | x-api-key | `claude-opus-5-5` |
| custom | responses or chat | user-entered base URL | bearer | user-entered |

The `JUSPRIN_OPENAI_ENDPOINT` override becomes `JUSPRIN_AGENT_ENDPOINT`, applied to whichever profile is active, with the old name kept as an alias so the shell harness keeps working.

### Setup and configuration

- `SetupCredentials` gains nothing new for the named providers. The custom row adds `endpoint` (already a field) and `family`.
- `ProviderKeySetup` and `load_agent_runtime` call one factory, `make_provider_agent(profile, credentials, transport)`, instead of naming the class. The probe stays what it is: one real request with no project data.
- AppConfig keys stay as they are: `<provider>_api_key`, `provider`, `model`. A custom provider adds `endpoint` and `family` under the same section.
- The setup page flips Anthropic to available, replaces "Other…" with OpenRouter plus a custom entry, and keeps "which model to use is decided for you" for the named rows.

### Tests

The 33 adapter tests split by what they assert:

- **Loop tests** (about 20: call ordering, unrun answers, refusals, images after results, skills once, late completion, cancellation, usage) run against `ProviderAgent` with a scripted fake codec, so a provider bug cannot hide a loop regression and vice versa.
- **Wire tests** (about 13: body shape, replay of earlier calls, title request, attachment import availability, SSE parsing, error mapping) become one file per codec. The Responses file keeps today's assertions byte for byte.
- **Conformance test**: one scripted turn (text, two calls, one failed result, an image, a fired skill, text) is driven through every codec with canned provider streams, and the sequence of `AgentEvent`s must be identical. This is the test that keeps the loop neutral as codecs are added.
- **Golden bodies**: `tests/project_prompt/requests.json` is the oracle for the Responses codec. A refactor that changes a recorded body is a refactor that changed behaviour.
- **Live smoke**, opt-in with keys: one real request per provider, checked for a text reply and one tool call. Wire drift only shows up live, so this runs before a release, not in CI.

### Rollout

1. **Extract, no behaviour change.** Split `OpenAIResponsesAgent` into `ProviderAgent` + `ResponsesCodec` + `ProviderProfile`. Keep `OpenAIResponsesAgent` as a one-line alias so the harness and tests compile untouched. Prove the recorded request bodies are byte-identical before and after.
2. **OpenRouter.** Add the profile row, the setup page entry, the live smoke. Decide the default model.
3. **Anthropic.** Add `AnthropicCodec` with the schema projection, the wire tests, the conformance test, the setup entry, the live smoke. Add `cache_creation` to `AgentUsage` so cost reporting shows cache writes.
4. **Chat Completions**, only when a concrete host that lacks a Responses endpoint is wanted. Ollama and LM Studio are the likely reasons.

## MCP clients: what changes and what does not

The question was whether the design must account for how MCP clients (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code, through the stdio bridge) use the tools. Checked against `Mcp/McpProtocol.cpp`, `Mcp/McpCatalog.cpp` and the tool extension guide:

- **Nothing in the MCP server depends on the LLM adapter**, and the reverse is also true. Both project `ToolRegistry` definitions: the MCP side into `tools/list` with annotations from `ActionClass`, the LLM side into provider tool definitions. `ToolExecutionCoordinator` runs both. The provider split touches neither.
- **The registry schema dialect is the one shared contract.** It is consumed by the registry validator, by OpenAI strict mode, by Anthropic strict mode, and by whatever model sits behind an MCP client. The Anthropic finding above (five rejected keywords) is handled by projection inside the Anthropic codec, so the registry keeps its full schemas for MCP clients and for native validation. Rewriting the registry to Anthropic's subset would weaken what every MCP client is told and what the validator checks. Projection is also what Anthropic's own SDK helpers do.
- **Images beside results already have a neutral home.** `ToolActivity.image` is one record; MCP returns it as an image content block, Anthropic puts it in the `tool_result`, Responses sends it as a following user message. The codec table above is the only place that knows the difference.
- **The in-app agent should not reach its tools through MCP.** Both Anthropic's MCP connector and OpenAI's `mcp` tool type need a server reachable from the provider's side; the embedded server is loopback-only by design. Direct registry projection stays.
- **Tool names** are snake_case ASCII in the registry, which satisfies Anthropic's and OpenAI's name rules without renaming, so MCP clients and the in-app agent keep seeing the same names.

## Things to verify before building

My hypotheses, not confirmed facts:

- Anthropic's accepted character set for `tool_use` ids. An earlier turn answered by OpenAI (`call_…`) or OpenRouter would be replayed to Anthropic if the user switches provider mid-conversation. If Anthropic constrains the id format, the across-turn replay must mint its own ids for foreign calls.
- Whether Anthropic accepts two consecutive user messages. The host emits file-load reports as user-role entries that can sit next to the user's own message. If not, the codec merges adjacent same-role entries.
- Whether OpenRouter's Responses endpoint honours `instructions`, `strict`, `parallel_tool_calls` and image parts inside `function_call_output`. Its tool-calling page shows `strict: null` and does not document the first three. The prompt evals already send `instructions` successfully, which covers one of them.
- Whether to enable Anthropic's server-side refusal fallback (`fallbacks: "default"` with the `server-side-fallback-2026-07-01` beta). It changes which model answers after a safety refusal, which is a product decision, so the design leaves it as a profile flag, off until decided.

## Sources

- [OpenRouter Responses API overview](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/responses/overview), [tool calling](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/responses/tool-calling), [reasoning](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/responses/reasoning)
- [Anthropic OpenAI SDK compatibility](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/cli-sdks-libraries/libraries/openai-sdk)
- [Anthropic strict tool use](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/strict-tool-use) and [structured outputs JSON Schema limitations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs)
- [OpenAI reasoning guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning)

| Setup page provider list | `AgentUI/src/components/Setup.tsx` | Lists Anthropic and Other as unavailable |
| Tool registry and MCP projection | `ToolRegistry.cpp`, `Mcp/McpProtocol.cpp` | Yes |

Three test surfaces read the Responses wire format directly: the 33 adapter tests in `tests/agent/test_openai_responses_agent.cpp`, the shell harness modes that record or hold request bodies (`tests/shell/shell_harness.cpp`, `project_prompt_scenario.inc`), and the Python prompt evals (`tests/project_prompt`, `tests/printer_prompt`), which replay recorded bodies against OpenRouter's Responses endpoint.

([overview](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/responses/overview), [tool calling](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/responses/tool-calling))
- **Anthropic's OpenAI-compatible endpoint is not a shortcut.** Anthropic's own page says it ignores `strict`, drops prompt caching, merges every system message into one, and is meant for testing, not production. ([OpenAI SDK compatibility](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/cli-sdks-libraries/libraries/openai-sdk)) Anthropic needs its native Messages API.
- **Anthropic strict mode rejects schema keywords the registry uses.** Unsupported: `minimum`, `maximum`, `multipleOf`, `minLength`, `maxLength`, and array constraints other than `minItems` of 0 or 1. ([structured outputs limitations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs)) OpenAI accepts these keywords today; the live harness runs prove it.
- **Within one turn, both APIs need the assistant's output echoed verbatim.** OpenAI returns reasoning items with `encrypted_content` under `store: false` and asks for them back with the function outputs. ([reasoning guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning)) Anthropic wants the full `content[]` of the assistant message, thinking blocks included, and on Claude Opus 5.5 and later a changed earlier turn invalidates thinking blocks.
```
IAgentService                      (unchanged)
  ProviderAgent                    the turn loop; today's OpenAIResponsesAgent minus the wire format
    IProviderCodec                 one per API family, pure JSON in and out, no network, no GUI
      ResponsesCodec               OpenAI, OpenRouter, any Responses-compatible host
      AnthropicCodec               Messages API
      ChatCompletionsCodec         later, only if a Chat-Completions-only host is wanted
    ProviderProfile                data: family, endpoint, auth style, default model, extra headers, error wording
    IAgentHttpTransport            unchanged, except headers become a list instead of one authorization string
```

### The loop and the transcript it owns

`ProviderAgent` keeps every rule the current class enforces, unchanged: one call runs at a time in the order written; a failed call answers the rest unrun; an unknown or invalid call is refused back to the model at most twice per turn; a result's image follows the results; fired skills ride on one request only; usage goes to the listener; a late event from a cancelled request is dropped by generation. All of that is expressed over a neutral transcript:

```
TurnTranscript
  instructions                      the session's text, byte-identical across the chat
  tools                             the ToolDefinitions offered this turn, plus skill_read's list
  opening                           earlier conversation (neutral records) + this turn's user content
  steps[]                           one per response so far:
    assistant_turn   json           opaque: output[] for Responses, content[] for Anthropic
    results[]                       call_id, state, output_json, optional image
    once[]                          skills fired by those results, sent on the next request only
```

The loop never looks inside `assistant_turn`. It gets the calls, the text deltas, the usage and the stop state from the codec's parsed events, and hands the opaque turn back to the same codec on the next request. A turn never changes provider, so the opaque value is always read by the codec that wrote it.

### The codec interface

Two functions, both deterministic and testable without a transport:

- `build(const TurnTranscript&, const ProviderProfile&, RequestKind) -> {body json, headers}`. `RequestKind` is the normal reply or the conversation-title request.
- `parse(const std::string& sse_data_payload) -> std::vector<StreamEvent>`. The loop keeps the SSE framing (it is identical across all three families) and passes each `data:` payload in. Events are neutral: `TextDelta`, `TurnComplete{assistant_turn, calls[], usage, stop}`, `Incomplete`, `Failed{code, retryable}`.

Anthropic's stream needs per-index accumulation of `input_json_delta` fragments before a call exists, so a codec is an object with a small amount of per-response state, reset by the loop at each request.

| Concern | ResponsesCodec (OpenAI, OpenRouter) | AnthropicCodec | ChatCompletionsCodec (later) |
|---|---|---|---|
| System prompt | `instructions` | top-level `system` with a `cache_control` breakpoint | first message, role system |
| App notes mid-conversation (today's developer role) | role `developer` | role `system` inside `messages` (Opus 5, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable; no beta header); for older models, a user text in the app's tag | role `system` on OpenAI; a tagged user text elsewhere, since hosts differ |
| Tool definition | `{type:function, name, parameters, strict}` | `{name, description, input_schema, strict}`, `cache_control` on the last tool | `{type:function, function:{...}}` |
| Strict | registry schema as is, `strict` when the object tree is closed (today's rule) | project the schema: move `minimum`, `maximum`, `minLength`, `maxLength`, `maxItems` and `minItems` above 1 into the property description, then `strict: true` | off by default; hosts vary |
| Tool result | `function_call_output` with a string `output` | `tool_result` with text and image blocks in one user message, all results of a response together | role `tool` messages, one per call |
| Image beside a result | separate user message after the results | image block inside the `tool_result` | separate user message |
| PDF attachment | `input_file` | `document` block, base64 | OpenRouter `file` part; otherwise text only |
| Streaming text | `response.output_text.delta` | `content_block_delta` with `text_delta` | `choices[0].delta.content` |
| Streaming calls | complete items in `response.completed` | `content_block_start` type `tool_use`, then `input_json_delta` fragments by index | `delta.tool_calls[i]` fragments by index |
| Terminal | `response.completed`, `incomplete`, `failed` | `message_delta` carries `stop_reason` and output usage; `message_stop` ends | `finish_reason` |
| Stop states | completed, incomplete | `end_turn`, `tool_use`, `max_tokens` (Incomplete), `refusal` (Failed, not retryable, with the category), `pause_turn` (resend) | `stop`, `tool_calls`, `length` |
| Usage | `input_tokens`, `input_tokens_details.cached_tokens` | `input_tokens`, `cache_read_input_tokens`, `cache_creation_input_tokens`, `output_tokens` | `prompt_tokens`, `prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`, with `stream_options.include_usage` |
| Prompt cache | automatic on a stable prefix | explicit: breakpoint on the last tool, the system text, and the last user message; tools, then system, then messages is the invalidation order | automatic on OpenAI; passed through on OpenRouter |
| Thinking | provider default | omit `thinking`; depth through `output_config.effort` from the profile | none |
| Required fields | none | `max_tokens` | none |
| Auth and version | `Authorization: Bearer` | `x-api-key`, `anthropic-version: 2023-06-01` | `Authorization: Bearer` |
| Idempotency | `Idempotency-Key` header | not documented; send nothing | not documented; send nothing |
| Errors | 401/403, 429, 5xx, timeout | the same plus 529 overloaded (retryable) and 413 | the same |

Error text today names OpenAI ("The OpenAI API key was rejected"). The display name moves into `ProviderProfile` so the wording is right for every provider without a per-provider branch.

### Provider profiles

A static table, one row per provider the setup page offers, plus a "custom" row the user fills in:

| id | family | endpoint | auth | default model |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| openai | responses | `https://api.openai.com/v1/responses` | bearer | `gpt-5.4-mini` (today's) |
| openrouter | responses | `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/responses` | bearer, plus `HTTP-Referer` and `X-Title` identifying JusPrin | to be chosen; the prompt evals use `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash` |
| anthropic | anthropic | `https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages` | x-api-key | `claude-opus-5-5` |
| custom | responses or chat | user-entered base URL | bearer | user-entered |

### Setup and configuration

- `SetupCredentials` gains nothing new for the named providers. The custom row adds `endpoint` (already a field) and `family`.
- `ProviderKeySetup` and `load_agent_runtime` call one factory, `make_provider_agent(profile, credentials, transport)`, instead of naming the class. The probe stays what it is: one real request with no project data.
- AppConfig keys stay as they are: `<provider>_api_key`, `provider`, `model`. A custom provider adds `endpoint` and `family` under the same section.
- The setup page flips Anthropic to available, replaces "Other…" with OpenRouter plus a custom entry, and keeps "which model to use is decided for you" for the named rows.

### Tests

The 33 adapter tests split by what they assert:

- **Loop tests** (about 20: call ordering, unrun answers, refusals, images after results, skills once, late completion, cancellation, usage) run against `ProviderAgent` with a scripted fake codec, so a provider bug cannot hide a loop regression and vice versa.
- **Wire tests** (about 13: body shape, replay of earlier calls, title request, attachment import availability, SSE parsing, error mapping) become one file per codec. The Responses file keeps today's assertions byte for byte.
- **Conformance test**: one scripted turn (text, two calls, one failed result, an image, a fired skill, text) is driven through every codec with canned provider streams, and the sequence of `AgentEvent`s must be identical. This is the test that keeps the loop neutral as codecs are added.
- **Golden bodies**: `tests/project_prompt/requests.json` is the oracle for the Responses codec. A refactor that changes a recorded body is a refactor that changed behaviour.
- **Live smoke**, opt-in with keys: one real request per provider, checked for a text reply and one tool call. Wire drift only shows up live, so this runs before a release, not in CI.

1. **Extract, no behaviour change.** Split `OpenAIResponsesAgent` into `ProviderAgent` + `ResponsesCodec` + `ProviderProfile`. Keep `OpenAIResponsesAgent` as a one-line alias so the harness and tests compile untouched. Prove the recorded request bodies are byte-identical before and after.
2. **OpenRouter.** Add the profile row, the setup page entry, the live smoke. Decide the default model.
3. **Anthropic.** Add `AnthropicCodec` with the schema projection, the wire tests, the conformance test, the setup entry, the live smoke. Add `cache_creation` to `AgentUsage` so cost reporting shows cache writes.
4. **Chat Completions**, only when a concrete host that lacks a Responses endpoint is wanted. Ollama and LM Studio are the likely reasons.

The question was whether the design must account for how MCP clients (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code, through the stdio bridge) use the tools. Checked against `Mcp/McpProtocol.cpp`, `Mcp/McpCatalog.cpp` and the tool extension guide:

- **Nothing in the MCP server depends on the LLM adapter**, and the reverse is also true. Both project `ToolRegistry` definitions: the MCP side into `tools/list` with annotations from `ActionClass`, the LLM side into provider tool definitions. `ToolExecutionCoordinator` runs both. The provider split touches neither.
- **The registry schema dialect is the one shared contract.** It is consumed by the registry validator, by OpenAI strict mode, by Anthropic strict mode, and by whatever model sits behind an MCP client. The Anthropic finding above (five rejected keywords) is handled by projection inside the Anthropic codec, so the registry keeps its full schemas for MCP clients and for native validation. Rewriting the registry to Anthropic's subset would weaken what every MCP client is told and what the validator checks. Projection is also what Anthropic's own SDK helpers do.
- **Images beside results already have a neutral home.** `ToolActivity.image` is one record; MCP returns it as an image content block, Anthropic puts it in the `tool_result`, Responses sends it as a following user message. The codec table above is the only place that knows the difference.
- **The in-app agent should not reach its tools through MCP.** Both Anthropic's MCP connector and OpenAI's `mcp` tool type need a server reachable from the provider's side; the embedded server is loopback-only by design. Direct registry projection stays.
- **Tool names** are snake_case ASCII in the registry, which satisfies Anthropic's and OpenAI's name rules without renaming, so MCP clients and the in-app agent keep seeing the same names.

## Things to verify before building

My hypotheses, not confirmed facts:

- Anthropic's accepted character set for `tool_use` ids. An earlier turn answered by OpenAI (`call_…`) or OpenRouter would be replayed to Anthropic if the user switches provider mid-conversation. If Anthropic constrains the id format, the across-turn replay must mint its own ids for foreign calls.
- Whether Anthropic accepts two consecutive user messages. The host emits file-load reports as user-role entries that can sit next to the user's own message. If not, the codec merges adjacent same-role entries.
- Whether OpenRouter's Responses endpoint honours `instructions`, `strict`, `parallel_tool_calls` and image parts inside `function_call_output`. Its tool-calling page shows `strict: null` and does not document the first three. The prompt evals already send `instructions` successfully, which covers one of them.
- Whether to enable Anthropic's server-side refusal fallback (`fallbacks: "default"` with the `server-side-fallback-2026-07-01` beta). It changes which model answers after a safety refusal, which is a product decision, so the design leaves it as a profile flag, off until decided.

## Sources

- [OpenRouter Responses API overview](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/responses/overview), [tool calling](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/responses/tool-calling), [reasoning](https://openrouter.ai/docs/api_reference/responses/reasoning)
- [Anthropic OpenAI SDK compatibility](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/cli-sdks-libraries/libraries/openai-sdk)
- [Anthropic strict tool use](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/strict-tool-use) and [structured outputs JSON Schema limitations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs)
- [OpenAI reasoning guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning)
